decree.title: The Decree on the Board
decree.text:
BY THE KING'S WILL

To avoid the misfortunes that light brings, it is commanded: put out the fires on the beacons, light no street lamps, stay indoors after sunset.

The darkness will pass on its own. Wait patiently.

The seal is almost worn away. Below, someone has added in charcoal, in a child's hand: "And when will it pass?"

oldrich_letter.title: An Unsent Letter
oldrich_letter.text:
Son,

I'm writing to you once again, and once again I don't know where to send it. They say it's dark in the city too. They say you're alive.

Things are the same here. The well creaks, Mara brews tea for empty benches, Borta hammers his anvil so as not to hear the silence.

I keep my father's lantern. I don't even know for whom. Perhaps for someone who won't be afraid.

Your father, Oldrich

lia_drawing.title: Lia's Drawing
lia_drawing.text:
A big yellow circle across the whole sheet, with rays in every direction — some of them curl like blades of grass. Below the circle are little houses, and from every chimney come not smoke, but flowers.

Signed in crooked letters: "THE SUN. WARM AND SMELLS OF GRASS. LIA".

vale_notes.title: The Herbalist's Notebook
vale_notes.text:
Mint — for worry. Thyme — for coughs. Glowcap — for dreams.

Noticed: the fireflies fly toward the beacon, though it has gone out. Not to a lantern, not to a campfire — to the beacon. As if they remember the warm wind.

The paths in the wood have led in circles ever since the fire was put out. The wood isn't wicked. The wood is lost. Like all of us.

I ought to go to the Ford. Take some mint to Mara. Tomorrow. Or the day after. Twenty years of "tomorrow".

soldier_letter.title: A Letter by an Old Stump
soldier_letter.text:
If you find this — don't judge too harshly.

There were six of us. They gave us buckets of sand and an order: put out the beacon in the wood. By the word of the king's councillor, they said — the light would call misfortune down from the mountains.

I was the last to bury the fire. The coals hissed like something alive. Then we got lost on the way back — the paths seemed to have shifted. Three days we walked in circles.

I keep thinking: what if the misfortune wasn't in the light? What if the misfortune is that we gave it up so easily?

Private Tim, forest guard

king_page.title: A Torn Diary Page
king_page.text:
…the councillor says again that the smoke from the mountains carries sickness, and the beacon fires draw it like moths.

I don't know. I remember my father taking me to the beacon above the capital, and the wind from the fire smelled of resin and bread.

But the councillor has never been wrong. Or do I simply not remember when he was wrong?

Today I signed the decree. My hand shook. Let the darkness pass on its own. Let it. I will wait.

(A beautiful hand, but the lines slide downward, as if the writer were very tired.)

ferry_log.title: The Ferry Book
ferry_log.text:
The ferryman's entries, in an uneven hand, by day.

"Ferried the herb-woman and her granddaughter. Fare — two onions."
"Ferried soldiers of the forest guard. Six. Gloomy. Fare — nothing, by decree."
"At night the king's councillor came. No torch. Three carts, crates under matting, smelling of burning. Ordered me to take them to the mountain trail and keep quiet. Paid in gold. Afterwards I couldn't bear to touch that gold — as if it were smeared with ash."
"The beacon above the mire was put out. Since then the lights over the bog burn brighter. Ferried no one more."

The rest of the pages are empty.

sealed_letter.title: A Letter with a Torn Seal
sealed_letter.text:
A scrap on the rotten boards, the seal with a crown torn off.

"…no one must see the mountains. If the beacons are lit again, the warm wind will drive the smoke away — and anyone with eyes will see that it still burns there, and why.

Tell the king that light brings misfortune. He will believe it: he is tired and wants to believe in something simple.

The smoke is our ally. Let it stand a hundred years.

Burn this letter."

It was not burned.

boot_drawing.title: A Child's Drawing in a Boot
boot_drawing.text:
In an old child's boot, tucked between the stones by the beacon — a folded sheet.

It shows a boat with a man holding a long pole, and around him frogs with enormous eyes, about twenty of them. Above it all — a beacon, with yellow lines going out in every direction.

Signed: "GRANDPA KORNEY AND THE FROGS. THEY SING WHEN IT'S LIGHT".

smoke_map.title: The Smoke Map
smoke_map.text:
A sheet pinned under a stone by the stairs. Ansar's hand.

On a map of the mountains — circles with dates. Under each: "smoke". Every year there are more circles, and all of them by the old silver mines.

In the margin: "There was a fire in the mountains twenty years ago. A forest fire burns out in a month. This one still burns. Which means someone is feeding it."

And below, large, underlined twice: "The Pall is not a misfortune fallen from the sky. The Pall is made."

palace_reply.title: A Reply from the Palace
palace_reply.text:
A scrap of a letter with the palace seal, caught in the rocks of the crag.

"To the scholar Ansar.

His Majesty does not receive. His Majesty is grieving and does not wish to hear of smoke.

The councillor bids us tell you: there are no more stars, a scholar has nothing to look at. The observatory is closed by decree. The beacons are put out for the good of the kingdom — light draws misfortune from the mountains.

Do not write again."

On the back — in a trembling hand, a different one, without a seal: "I didn't know. Forgive me. — R."

ansar_journal.title: The Observation Journal
ansar_journal.text:
The last pages of Ansar's journal.

"Twenty years ago Councillor Morn found silver in the mountains. The mines bit into a coal seam, and the seam caught fire underground. Such a fire cannot be put out — it can only stop being fed.

But Morn did not stop. He smelts silver on the underground heat, and the smoke rises as the Pall. The ancestors built the beacons so that a warm wind would drive the smoke from the mountains — and with it the mines and furnaces would be revealed. That is why the beacons had to go out.

The king was told: light draws misfortune. The king had just buried the queen — he would have believed anything, so long as he did not have to decide anything himself.

I wrote to the palace seven times. They answered once.

If whoever reads this journal carries fire — bear the king no grudge. He is not wicked. He is tired and left alone. And loneliness and fear often wear the same cloak."

fresco_beacons.title: Fresco: Five Fires
fresco_beacons.text:
A faded painting: hills, a light sky, the sun. On the hills — five towers, and above each a red fire. Below — people, very small, reaching toward the fires with little stroke-arms.

The paint has crumbled, but the sun is clearly visible. Someone once painted over it with charcoal — and the charcoal wore away before the paint did.

fresco_mine.title: Fresco: The Mountain and the Smoke
fresco_mine.text:
A mountain with the black mouth of a mine. Inside — a red dot of fire. From the mountain rise clouds of smoke, higher and wider.

On the right — a figure in a dark cloak, something silver in its hand. The figure's face has been carefully scraped away. Not by time — by a knife.

fresco_grief.title: Fresco: Two Thrones
fresco_grief.text:
The throne hall. Two thrones side by side: on one, the king in red, wearing a crown. The second throne is empty, and a single candle burns beside it.

Behind the king, in the shadow of a column — a dark figure. It is bending close to the king's ear.

The paint on the king's face has hardly faded. As if the painter tried very hard to show how heavy it was for him.

fresco_dark.title: Fresco: The Fires Gone Out
fresco_dark.text:
The same five towers — but there are no fires above them. The sky is painted dark. The houses below have their shutters closed tight.

In the corner — a long dark figure without a face. It was added later, in different paint, clumsily. As if whoever did it wanted the truth known — but was afraid to sign it.

guard_note.title: A Sentry's Note
guard_note.text:
Scratched on the back of a duty roster.

"The king isn't sleeping again. He walks the hall with a candle and talks to the empty throne. He ordered that no one be let in — not the physician, not the cook.

Councillor Morn went to the mountains and never came back. They say it's warmer for him there.

We leave tomorrow. All of us. The darkness here is such that it seems to be watching.

If someone comes with fire — don't fear the king. Fear how completely alone he has become."

king_diary.title: The Last Page
king_diary.text:
A sheet pinned under a candlestick by the throne. The same hand as the diary from the wood, but the letters are larger and more uneven, like those of a very old man.

"Today I dreamed of a window. She opened it, and a wind came into the room, warm, smelling of bread.

I woke and went to open the window in the hall. But the window is boarded up. I ordered it so myself.

If someone comes with fire — I will shout. I know myself. Let him not listen to what I shout. Let him listen to what I keep silent about."

Below, very small: "I am so tired of being afraid."
